paras: The attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Indiana, was a night raid on August 11, 1880, in which masked men broke into the house of Mack, a Black man, threatened to hang him and ordered him to leave the county. Mack was released on a promise to leave but resolved to stay, and papers reported the attack as part of election-season efforts to drive Black residents out of Indiana.

Mack lived about a mile from Columbus on a farm rented by a Mr. Walker, and both reports described him as "inoffensive." A Cincinnati dispatch of August 12 said that "Demeratic [Democratic] threats of driving the negroes out of Indiana" were being carried out in at least three counties.

Early on the morning of August 11, according to that dispatch, a "band of masked Kuklux" broke open the door and windows of Mack's house and dragged him from his bed. The men swore that they would hang him and that they meant to "clean out all the niggers in the county before the election." They searched the house for arms, found none, and agreed to let Mack go on condition that he leave at once.
The band then rode off with others waiting in the road. Soon afterward Walker's house was stoned, with the party yelling, cursing and threatening around it for a considerable time.
The Indianapolis Leader reported that Mack, though made to promise to leave the county, had "made up his mind" not to do so. No report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The earliest report was a three-sentence brief in the Indianapolis Leader on August 14, which said a "crowd of masked men" had maltreated Mack. The Leader closed by blaming the Sentinel: "Thus is the Sentinel's savage appeal bearing fruit." The fuller Cincinnati dispatch reached the Somerset Herald in Pennsylvania on August 25 under the headline "Intimidation in Indiana," framing it as Democratic intimidation and noting similar attempts at Bluffton and Shelbyville.
Both papers condemned the attack and stressed Mack's innocence, but only the dispatch used the label "Kuklux" and quoted the band's slur.

reader.title: Attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Indiana
bases: A masked band broke into a Black man's house, threatened to hang him and ordered him out of the county, with a stated aim of driving Black residents out before the election; no one was killed (A1, A2).

Mack was threatened with hanging but released on a promise to leave, and no death is reported (A1, A2); the band acted without lawful authority, and its stated aim was to 'clean out' Black residents before the election rather than to punish a crime (A2).

An Indianapolis brief (A1) and a Cincinnati dispatch reprinted in Pennsylvania (A2) agree that masked men attacked Joshua Mack near Columbus and forced a promise that he leave, though they differ in detail.

accounts.label: Cincinnati wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Masked 'Kuklux' broke into Mack's house, threatened to hang him and to 'clean out' Black residents before the election, searched for arms, let him go on condition he leave, and stoned his landlord's house.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Leader called Mack 'inoffensive' and said the attack showed 'the Sentinel's savage appeal bearing fruit'.
The Somerset Herald ran the Cincinnati dispatch under 'Intimidation in Indiana', framing it as Democratic threats to drive Black people out of the state, with 'vile oaths' from the band.
